meeting_header:
Date: 2026-05-04 14:00 UTC | Duration: 74 mins | Location: Zoom | Recording: available
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Luca Romano (Redwood SE), Carlos Herrera (Elysian CTO), Anika Bose (Elysian ML Eng), Ravi Kumar (Elysian SRE), Tess Nguyen (Elysian Platform)
summary: Deep dive into cross-region streaming stalls observed by Elysian. Primary hypothesis: sporadic KV fetch stalls + VPC edge proxy serialization causing p95->p99 amplification under streaming. Agreed to run dedicated trace capture, share shard map, and test streaming fallback and quantization profiles. SE to provide runbook and config diffs.
topics: runtime performance, p95/p99 tail, streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache hot shards, batching tradeoffs, quantization profiles (int8/Q4), VPC networking / NAT asymmetry, cross-region proxy serialization, observability traces
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Park: ok everybody, thanks for hopping on. we saw the incident details Carlos shared—looks like p95 is fine but p99 spikes to 1.2s when streaming is enabled. can you walk us through what you saw?
[00:18] Carlos Herrera: yeah, uh hi all. so on 2026-05-02 we saw an increase in user-facing latency, mostly during cross-region requests coming out of eu-west to us-east, and it correlated with streaming endpoints. non-streaming had a smaller tail. logs show stalled kv fetches and some proxy queuing.
[00:40] Maya Chen: when you say kv fetch stalls, is that per-shard or a single hotkey? do you have qps per shard?
[00:51] Anika Bose: rough numbers, at peak our model requester sends ~120 req/s, and the shard map shows two shards taking 60% of requests — looks like hotshard behavior. we also saw serialization at the vpc egress proxy, the envoy logs show 40-60ms serialization bursts that amplify under streaming.
[01:14] Luca Romano: interesting — serialization at the proxy + small kv stalls can multiply in streaming since streaming maintains open loops for each token and small delays cascade. in non-streaming the client waits less often? sorry, that sounded weird — basically batching boundaries are different.
[01:40] Ravi Kumar: yes, the streaming path keeps the connection open and we stream partial tokens. when the kv cache misses or returns late by 30-80ms, that adds to the token emit timing and you see p99 blow up. also noticed NAT/timeouts in cross-region path, maybe asymmetric routing adding jitter.
[02:05] Jordan Park: right. our runtime has an internal metric for 'kv-latency-ms' per request; can you share traces where kv-latency spikes align with proxy serialization? a pcap would be ideal.
[02:22] Carlos Herrera: we'll share the trace IDs. question — would changing to non-streaming be an immediate mitigation? we worry about UX.
[02:33] Maya Chen: non-streaming typically reduces the number of small network round trips; you lose perceived latency (users see finished output later) but it can reduce tail amplification because tokens aren't emitted as soon as they're available. in practice, for very chatty workloads non-streaming reduced p99 by ~30% in our tests.
[02:58] Anika Bose: what's the batching tradeoff — if we increase batch size at the runtime, will that help?
[03:07] Luca Romano: batching helps amortize kernel overhead but increases latency for the first token. for tail, batching can help if the KV stall is per-request: if one request waits, it doesn't hold other already-ready requests, but if a hot shard creates queuing in the KV layer that backs up the runtime, batching alone won't fix it. we should look at shard placement and move hot keys, or enable per-shard rate limiting and local caching.
[03:43] Ravi Kumar: we use a managed Redis-like KV behind our VPC; we currently have 3 replicas across regions and consistent hashing. we saw a failure of a replica (brief) which bumped traffic to a single node on a different AZ and increased latency.
[04:05] Jordan Park: that matches: cross-region failover + retransmit + proxy serialization becomes a multi-hop problem. let's define a short experiment set: 1) reproduce at low load with packet capture and detailed runtime traces 2) stream vs non-stream compare at 100 req/s 3) vary quantization and batch sizes to measure p95/p99 tradeoffs.
[04:28] Carlos Herrera: agreed. also, we want to test int8 vs q4x4 quantization — does Redwood recommend particular profiles for streaming?
[04:40] Maya Chen: for streaming we tend to prefer q4 variants that preserve early token quality and reduce token compute time. int8 can save cycles but in some kernels it increases jitter because of different kernel paths — you'll want to run both. our Optimize team can suggest profiles per model.
[05:00] Anika Bose: ok — observability — what traces do you need from us?
[05:07] Jordan Park: ideally 1) packet captures at the VPC egress for a 30-60 minute window around an incident 2) runtime debug traces (we'll provide a trace collector command) 3) list of request IDs and timestamps 4) kv shard mapping image. you can drop links in the CRM ticket.
[05:26] Ravi Kumar: noted. port knock: we also suspect that our VPC proxy (a sidecar) serializes streaming frames which causes small head-of-line delays. is there a recommended proxy tuning?
[05:38] Luca Romano: yes — increase connection-concurrency, enable chunked transfer optimizations, and disable per-chunk Nagle-like coalescing. also consider moving streaming termination closer to the runtime via a regional edge proxy to avoid cross-region egress serialization.
[05:59] Carlos Herrera: is there a quick mitigation we can flip while we investigate?
[06:05] Maya Chen: two quick mitigations: 1) fall back streaming to non-streaming for cross-region traffic (config toggle per-route) 2) enable local prefix/KV caching for the most common hot keys, even a tiny LRU of 128 entries reduces KV hits. we can roll both as config toggles and measure.
[06:24] Anika Bose: okay let's talk metrics to watch.
[06:30] Jordan Park: watch per-token latency distribution, kv-latency histogram, runtime queue depth, and proxy serialization time. also monitor p50/p95/p99 and the delta between streaming and non-streaming.
[06:42] Ravi Kumar: we'll also capture tcp retransmits and jitter between regions.
[06:46] [Crosstalk] Tess Nguyen: and the customer impact — some cohorts saw higher error rates during spikes, not just latency.
[06:55] Luca Romano: error rates often follow tail latency because clients time out and retransmit; small token-level delays cascade. that's why safe fallback is important.
[07:06] Jordan Park: ok, schedule: we'll do an initial reproduce next week. Maya, Luca — can you prepare a short runbook and the config diff for toggling streaming fallback and enabling local cache?
[07:16] Maya Chen: yep, will do. I'll include the telemetry queries.
[07:19] Luca Romano: I'll add recommended quantization profiles and a checklist for kernel selection impacts. note: some quantized kernels change attention memory patterns and that can change KV payload sizes a bit.
[07:34] Anika Bose: quick question on billing/throughput — if we switch to non-streaming, does that materially change cost?
[07:41] Jordan Park: it can reduce token overhead for many tiny emissions but it may increase average latency and slightly increase per-request cost if more compute happens at once. we'll model cost for both and include a projection in the follow-up.
[08:00] Carlos Herrera: any concerns about Dedicated vs Private for this? we are evaluating on-prem later this year.
[08:07] Maya Chen: on-prem gives you full control of the network so cross-region is less of an issue internally, but you still need to manage shard placement and hot keys. Dedicated in our infra can be pinned to a single region to avoid cross-region egress. Private/VPC gives stronger controls but increases ops overhead.
[08:28] Ravi Kumar: for now we'd like Redwood to run the reproduce on a Dedicated test pool so we can compare with our infra.
[08:35] Jordan Park: fine with that — we'll spin up a dedicated pool with identical model and region pairing. please upload sample request IDs and the shard map.
[08:44] [15:00] Maya Chen: (sharing screen) here's a sketch — when streaming, token emission is gated on multiple components: model token readiness, kv prefix fetch, network wraps. a small delay in any leads to distribution tail.
[15:32] Anika Bose: hmm ok that visual makes sense — can we instrument per-token timers?
[15:40] Luca Romano: yes, the runtime can emit per-token timing events at debug level, though it adds overhead. we recommend sampling 1% of requests with per-token traces.
[17:12] Carlos Herrera: are there known kernel path instabilities with q4 variants causing jitter?
[17:20] Maya Chen: sometimes. quantization changes the execution kernels; some GPUs schedule small kernels differently which increases variance. it's model & hardware specific. that's why we test both.
[20:00] Ravi Kumar: ok last bit — do you have a template for the streaming fallback policy?
[20:08] Jordan Park: yes, we'll share a policy template: criteria (cross-region, p99>500ms for 5 minutes), actions (toggle non-streaming, increase batching to N=4, enable local cache), rollback (auto revert after 10 minutes if p99 < 400ms). we'll attach to the ticket.
[20:30] Carlos Herrera: great. thanks all.
[20:35] Jordan Park: recap: Redwood to run traces on Dedicated pool, Elysian to share shard map & traces, SEs to produce runbook+profiles, schedule follow-up on 2026-05-11. meeting notes and attachments will be added to CRM ticket.
[20:50] [END]
